Notifications

Source: vignettes/notifications.Rmd
notifications.Rmd

EpiSODIC can notify your team whenever episodic_run_cron() detects new clusters or when a detection run fails. Notifications are entirely optional: if you do not configure them, the system continues to work exactly as before, and you review clusters through the dashboard alone.

Supported channels:

Channel Transport Needs R package
ntfy HTTP POST to a self-hosted or public ntfy server httr2
SMTP Any SMTP server (Gmail, Outlook, institutional relay, etc.) curl
sendmail The sendmail binary on a Linux/Unix server (none)
Microsoft 365 Microsoft Graph API (application or delegated auth) Microsoft365R, AzureGraph
Teams Power Automate Workflow webhook (Adaptive Card) httr2
Slack Incoming Webhook httr2

You can enable as many channels in parallel as you like. Each channel is independent: if one fails, the others still send, and a notification failure never rolls back a successful detection run.

Where to configure

Notification settings go in your instance YAML configuration file, the same file that EPISODIC_CONFIG points at (see vignette("environment-variables")). Add a notifications key at the top level. The shipped inst/config/default.yaml contains commented-out examples for every channel; copy the ones you need into your instance file and fill in the values.

Notification configuration is deliberately excluded from the detection config_hash. This means:

  • Changing notification settings never alters detection reproducibility.
  • Secrets (passwords, webhook URLs, client secrets) never reach the config_snapshot stored on each run.

Minimal example: ntfy

ntfy is the simplest channel to set up. If you run your own ntfy server, or use the public instance at ntfy.sh, this is all you need in your instance YAML:

notifications:
  enabled: true
  triggers:
    new_clusters: true
    run_failure: true
  channels:
    ntfy:
      enabled: true
      server: "https://ntfy.sh"
      topic: "my-episodic-alerts"

That is it. Install httr2 (install.packages("httr2")) and test:

episodic_notify_test()

Subscribe to the topic my-episodic-alerts in the ntfy app on your phone or desktop, and you will see the test message arrive.

ntfy with authentication

If your ntfy server requires a login:

    ntfy:
      enabled: true
      server: "https://ntfy.example.org"
      topic: "episodic-alerts"
      priority: 4            # ntfy priority 1 (min) to 5 (max); default 4 (high)
      auth:
        username: "episodic"
        password: "s3cr3t"

SMTP (Gmail, institutional relay, any SMTP server)

Works with any SMTP server that supports STARTTLS. For Gmail, create an App Password (requires 2FA on the Google account) and use that instead of the account password.

    smtp:
      enabled: true
      host: "smtp.gmail.com"
      port: 587
      tls: true
      username: "episodic.alerts@gmail.com"
      password: "xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx"   # Gmail App Password
      from: "episodic.alerts@gmail.com"
      to:
        - "team-lead@example.org"
        - "oncall@example.org"

For an institutional relay that does not require authentication (common on internal networks):

    smtp:
      enabled: true
      host: "mail-relay.internal.example.org"
      port: 25
      tls: false
      from: "episodic@example.org"
      to:
        - "epi-team@example.org"

Requires the curl package (install.packages("curl")).

sendmail (Linux/Unix)

If the server running EpiSODIC has sendmail (or a compatible MTA such as Postfix or msmtp) installed and configured, you can pipe messages directly without needing an external SMTP server:

    sendmail:
      enabled: true
      binary: "/usr/sbin/sendmail"    # default; change if your MTA is elsewhere
      from: "episodic@example.org"
      to:
        - "epi-team@example.org"

No additional R packages required. The binary must be executable by the user running the cron job.

Microsoft 365

Sends email through the Microsoft Graph API. Two authentication flows are supported, depending on your Azure AD (Entra ID) setup.

Option A: App-only (client credentials) – recommended for unattended cron

This is the recommended approach for a cron job. It requires an Azure AD app registration with the Mail.Send application permission (admin-consented).

  1. In the Azure portal, go to Azure Active Directory > App registrations > New registration.
  2. Name it (e.g. “EpiSODIC Notifications”), set Supported account types to “Accounts in this organizational directory only”.
  3. Under API permissions, add Microsoft Graph > Application permissions > Mail.Send. Click Grant admin consent.
  4. Under Certificates & secrets, create a new client secret and copy it immediately.
    microsoft365:
      enabled: true
      tenant_id: "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      client_id: "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      client_secret: "your-client-secret-value"
      from: "episodic@example.org"    # must be a mailbox the app is authorised to send from
      to:
        - "team-lead@example.org"

Option B: Delegated (cached interactive token)

If you cannot get admin consent for application-level permissions, or if your organisation restricts app-only mail sending, you can use a delegated token instead. This requires a one-time interactive login on the server:

episodic_setup_microsoft365(
  tenant_id = "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
  client_id = "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"  # optional; uses the Microsoft365R default if NULL
)

This opens a browser window (or prints a device-code URL for headless servers). Sign in with the account that will send notifications. The token is cached in ~/.local/share/AzureR/ and reused by subsequent cron runs.

In your instance YAML, omit client_secret:

    microsoft365:
      enabled: true
      tenant_id: "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      client_id: "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      from: "episodic@example.org"
      to:
        - "team-lead@example.org"

Token lifetime: Delegated refresh tokens typically expire after 90 days of inactivity. If the cron runs at least once within that window, the token refreshes itself automatically. If the token does expire, re-run episodic_setup_microsoft365().

Requires Microsoft365R and AzureGraph (install.packages(c("Microsoft365R", "AzureGraph"))).

Microsoft Teams

Teams notifications use a Power Automate Workflow webhook. The legacy Office 365 Connector webhooks are deprecated by Microsoft and should not be used for new setups.

Setting up the webhook

  1. In Teams, go to the channel where you want notifications.
  2. Click … (more options) > Workflows.
  3. Search for “Post to a channel when a webhook request is received” and select it.
  4. Follow the prompts. When done, copy the webhook URL (it looks like https://*.logic.azure.com/workflows/...).
    teams:
      enabled: true
      webhook_url: "https://prod-XX.westeurope.logic.azure.com/workflows/..."

The notification is sent as an Adaptive Card, which renders as a structured card in the Teams channel with pathogen, location, case counts, and a link to the dashboard.

Requires httr2 (install.packages("httr2")).

Slack

Slack notifications use an Incoming Webhook.

Setting up the webhook

  1. Go to api.slack.com/apps and create a new app (or use an existing one).
  2. Under Incoming Webhooks, activate them and click Add New Webhook to Workspace.
  3. Choose the channel and copy the webhook URL.
    slack:
      enabled: true
      webhook_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/<workspace-id>/<bot-id>/<token>"

The notification is formatted as Slack mrkdwn, with pathogen names in bold, case counts, and (if configured) a link to the dashboard.

Requires httr2 (install.packages("httr2")).

Triggers

Two triggers are available. Both are independently toggleable:

Trigger Fires when Default
new_clusters The cron run created at least one new cluster Must be explicitly set to true
run_failure The cron run’s status is "failed" Must be explicitly set to true 
notifications:
  enabled: true
  triggers:
    new_clusters: true
    run_failure: true

If both triggers fire on the same run (new clusters were detected, but something else in the run also failed), two separate notifications are sent.

Dashboard link

If your EpiSODIC dashboard is reachable at a URL, set dashboard_url and every notification will include a direct link:

notifications:
  enabled: true
  dashboard_url: "https://episodic.example.org"
  # ...channels...

This produces a clickable link in email bodies, a button in the Teams Adaptive Card, and a hyperlink in Slack messages.

Full reference example

Below is a complete notifications block with every channel shown. Copy only what you need.

notifications:
  enabled: true
  dashboard_url: "https://episodic.example.org"
  triggers:
    new_clusters: true
    run_failure: true
  channels:
    ntfy:
      enabled: true
      server: "https://ntfy.example.org"
      topic: "episodic-alerts"
      priority: 4
      auth:
        username: "episodic"
        password: "s3cr3t"
    smtp:
      enabled: false
      host: "smtp.gmail.com"
      port: 587
      tls: true
      username: "episodic.alerts@gmail.com"
      password: "xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx"
      from: "episodic.alerts@gmail.com"
      to:
        - "team-lead@example.org"
        - "oncall@example.org"
    sendmail:
      enabled: false
      binary: "/usr/sbin/sendmail"
      from: "episodic@example.org"
      to:
        - "epi-team@example.org"
    microsoft365:
      enabled: false
      tenant_id: "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      client_id: "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      client_secret: "your-client-secret-value"
      from: "episodic@example.org"
      to:
        - "team-lead@example.org"
    teams:
      enabled: false
      webhook_url: "https://prod-XX.westeurope.logic.azure.com/workflows/..."
    slack:
      enabled: false
      webhook_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/<workspace-id>/<bot-id>/<token>"

Testing your setup

After configuring notifications, always run the test function interactively before relying on cron:

episodic_notify_test()

This validates the configuration (checking for missing required fields and uninstalled packages), then sends a test message through every enabled channel. It reports success or failure per channel with the exact error message, so you can fix problems before the next real run.

What a notification looks like

New clusters

The notification includes, for each new cluster (up to 10, with a “+N more” summary for the rest):

  • Pathogen name
  • Location: institution, ward, and/or region, depending on the stream level
  • Cases: observed count, expected count, and their ratio
  • Priority score: the composite score that ranks the cluster
  • Period: first and last day of the detection window

The subject line reads: EpiSODIC: 3 new cluster(s) detected on 2025-09-01

Run failure

The notification includes the date, the hostname of the server that ran the detection, and the error message. This lets you triage whether the failure is a data problem, a configuration problem, or a server issue before you check any logs.

Troubleshooting

“Notifications are not enabled in the configuration” when calling episodic_notify_test(): Check that your instance YAML has notifications: enabled: true and that EPISODIC_CONFIG points at that file.

Channel sends succeed in the test but do not fire on cron runs: Check the triggers section. Both new_clusters and run_failure must be explicitly set to true; they do not default to on.

SMTP connection times out: Ensure the server can reach the SMTP host and port. Firewalls, VPNs, and cloud-provider restrictions on outbound port 25/587 are common causes.

Microsoft 365 “Insufficient privileges”: For app-only auth, the Mail.Send application permission must have admin consent. For delegated auth, the signed-in user must have a mailbox and the Mail.Send delegated permission on the app registration.

Teams webhook returns 202 but no card appears: Power Automate Workflow webhooks can silently drop malformed payloads. Check that the webhook URL is correct and that the workflow is turned on in Power Automate.

Slack webhook returns invalid_payload: Ensure httr2 is installed and up to date. The payload is JSON with a single text field; the webhook URL must be an Incoming Webhook, not a Slack API endpoint.
